principle: Visibility of system status: keep users informed about what is happening through timely feedback.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: Trigger each action on screen; feedback (loading, selected, saved state) is visible within about 1 second.
bad: Submit button tapped, nothing changes for 3 seconds, no spinner.
good: Button shows progress state, then a visible 'Saved' confirmation.

principle: Match between system and the real world: use words and conventions familiar to users, not internal jargon.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: List every label on screen; each uses words the target user would say, with no internal or system terms.
bad: Button reads 'Instantiate workspace'.
good: Button reads 'Create project'.

principle: User control and freedom: give clearly labeled ways to back out of or undo unwanted actions.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: In each modal, flow step or destructive action, find a visible cancel, back, close or undo control.
bad: Full-screen modal with no close button.
good: Modal has a visible Cancel and an Undo toast after delete.

principle: Consistency and standards: uniform terms and actions within the product, aligned with platform and industry conventions.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: Compare repeated elements (buttons, links, icons, labels) across the screens; the same function looks and reads the same.
bad: 'Save' on one form, 'Submit' on another, 'Done' on a third, all styled differently.
good: One label and one style per action across the product.

principle: Error prevention: design out error-prone conditions or confirm risky actions before commitment.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: Find destructive or irreversible actions; each has a confirmation, undo, or constrained input.
bad: Free-text date field that accepts 'tomorrow-ish'; Delete with no confirmation.
good: Date picker, plus a confirmation that names what will be deleted.

principle: Recognition rather than recall: make options and information visible so users need not remember them.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: Check that needed info (context, options, prior choices) is on screen, not required from memory of another screen.
bad: Checkout step 3 asks for a code shown only on step 1.
good: Code and summary are visible on the step that needs them.

principle: Flexibility and efficiency of use: offer shortcuts or tailoring for frequent actions without burdening novices.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: Look for accelerators (search, shortcuts, saved/recent items, bulk actions) on repeated-use screens.
bad: Power-user list screen with no search, filter or bulk select.
good: Search, filters and multi-select available but unobtrusive.

principle: Aesthetic and minimalist design: remove irrelevant or rarely needed content so essential information stands out.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: Point at each element; it supports the screen's main task, or it is removable.
bad: Dashboard with 14 equal-weight widgets and promo banners.
good: Three key metrics prominent, the rest behind progressive disclosure.

principle: Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors: plain language, pinpoint the problem, suggest a fix.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: For each visible error, check it states what failed, in plain words, and what to do next.
bad: 'Error 500'.
good: 'We couldn't save your changes. Check your connection and try again.'

principle: Help and documentation: task-focused, searchable help with concrete steps, ideally in context.
source: NN/g 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
test: On complex or unfamiliar steps, check for in-context help (hint text, help link) that names concrete steps.
bad: Complex form field with no hint or help link.
good: Field has a one-line hint and a link to a short how-to.

principle: WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text content: meaningful images and icons have a text alternative that serves the same purpose.
test: Inspect the accessibility tree: each informative image/icon has a non-empty alt or label; decorative ones are hidden.
bad: Icon-only button with no accessible name.
good: Icon button labelled 'Search'; decorative divider hidden from AT.

principle: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and relationships: structure shown visually (headings, lists, form labels, tables) is also programmatically determinable.
test: Compare visual headings, lists, labels with the DOM/accessibility tree; each visual structure has matching semantics.
bad: Heading styled with a bold div; input with a visually adjacent but unassociated label.
good: h2 element for section titles; label bound to its input.

principle: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of color: color is not the only visual means of conveying information.
test: Desaturate the screenshot; status, errors, links and required fields must still be distinguishable.
bad: Error field marked only by a red border; links distinguished only by color.
good: Red border plus an error icon and text; links underlined.

principle: WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum): text contrast is at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text (18pt or 14pt bold).
test: Measure foreground vs background of each text style, including grey placeholder and disabled-looking text that is hard to read; ratio >= 4.5:1 (3:1 if large).
bad: Grey text on white that is hard to read: light grey (#999) on white, 2.8:1.

principle: WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text: text can be resized to 200% without loss of content or functionality.
test: Zoom text to 200%; nothing is clipped, overlapping or hidden, and all controls remain usable.
bad: Fixed-height container clips text at 200%.
good: Container grows with text.

principle: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow: content reflows at 320 CSS px width with no horizontal scrolling (two-dimensional scrolling).
test: Set viewport to 320 CSS px wide; page has no horizontal scrollbar and no content is cut off.
bad: Wide table forces horizontal page scroll on phone.
good: Layout stacks to one column at 320px.

principle: WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: UI component boundaries/states and meaningful graphics have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors.
test: Measure input borders, icon glyphs, focus/selected states against their background; each >= 3:1.
bad: Pale grey (#ddd) input border on white.
good: #767676 or darker border.

principle: WCAG 1.4.12 Text Spacing: content stays readable when line height is 1.5x, paragraph spacing 2x, letter spacing 0.12x and word spacing 0.16x font size.
test: Apply the four spacing overrides; no text is clipped or overlaps.
bad: Fixed-height button clips its label when letter-spacing grows.
good: Containers use min-height and flexible padding.

principle: WCAG 2.4.4 Link Purpose (In Context): the purpose of each link can be determined from its text or its context.
test: Read link texts out of context; each says where it goes or what it does.
bad: Several links reading 'Click here' or 'Read more'.
good: 'Read the pricing guide'.

principle: WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels: headings and labels describe the topic or purpose.
test: Skim headings and form labels only; each describes its section or field.
bad: Heading 'Details' above unrelated content; label 'Field 1'.
good: Heading 'Shipping address'; label 'Email address'.

principle: WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible: any keyboard-operable control has a visible focus indicator.
test: Tab through the page; every focusable element shows a visible focus state.
bad: outline: none with no replacement.
good: 2px focus ring with 3:1 contrast.

principle: WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum): a focused control is not entirely hidden by author-created content such as sticky headers or cookie banners.
test: Tab through the page with sticky elements present; the focused element is never fully covered.
bad: Sticky footer covers the focused input.
good: scroll-padding keeps focused items clear of sticky bars.

principle: WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum): pointer targets are at least 24x24 CSS px, unless spacing or another exception applies.
test: Measure the bounding box of each link, button, icon control; width and height >= 24 CSS px (or 24px circle of free space).
bad: Button too small to tap with a pointer: 16px close icon with no padding.
good: 24px+ hit area; 44px preferred on touch.

principle: WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification: detected input errors identify the item in error and describe the error in text.
test: Trigger validation; the faulty field is identified and the error is described in text near it.
bad: Red outline only, no message.
good: 'Email address is missing the @' under the field.

principle: WCAG 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions: labels or instructions are provided where content requires user input.
test: Each input has a persistent visible label or instruction, not only placeholder text.
bad: Placeholder-only 'Email' that vanishes when typing.
good: Visible label above the field.

principle: WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value: every UI component exposes a programmatic name and role, and its state/value changes are available to assistive tech.
test: Inspect the accessibility tree; each control has a name, role and current state (expanded, checked, selected).
bad: div with onclick and no role or name.
good: button element with aria-expanded kept in sync.

principle: Offer sufficiently sized controls: iOS default control size is 44x44 pt (minimum 28x28 pt).
test: Measure each tappable control (button, icon, row) in points; it should be >= 44x44 pt and never below 28x28 pt, so it is not too small to tap.
bad: Button too small to tap: 24pt icon button in a nav bar with no extra hit area.
good: Button big enough to tap: 44x44 pt tappable frame around a 24pt glyph.

principle: Support Dynamic Type: use text styles and keep text legible and untruncated at larger accessibility sizes.
test: Render at the largest accessibility text size; text is not clipped or truncated, hierarchy is preserved, layout reflows.
bad: Fixed 14pt labels that do not scale and clip at large sizes.
good: Text styles; columns reduce as text grows.

principle: Support both appearance modes with semantic/adaptive colors and at least 4.5:1 contrast in each.
test: Render light and dark; text/icons stay legible (>= 4.5:1) and no hard-coded light surfaces appear in dark mode.
bad: White card with dark text left in dark mode; dark grey text on near-black.
good: System background and label colors adapt.

principle: Use a tab bar for top-level navigation only, with few tabs and short labels; avoid overflow More tab.
test: Inspect the tab bar: tabs navigate (not act), each has a label, and there is no 'More' overflow.
bad: Tab bar with a 'Add' action tab and 7 tabs including More.
good: 4 to 5 tabs with single-word labels.

principle: Sheets are for simple, focused tasks; show one at a time with Cancel/Done (never Done alone) and swipe-to-dismiss.
test: Open each sheet: it holds a short task, shows Cancel (leading) and Done (trailing) or a close control, and is not stacked on another sheet.
bad: Sheet with only a Done button, or a multi-step wizard in a sheet.
good: Cancel on the leading edge, Done on the trailing edge.

principle: Use SF Symbols that match adjacent text weight and scale and use system colors.
test: Compare icon stroke weight and size with adjacent text; they should match, with consistent variant (outline in toolbars, fill in tab bars).
bad: Thin custom icon next to bold label; mixed icon styles.
good: SF Symbol weight matched to its label.

principle: Use alerts sparingly, for essential information with clear titles and specific button labels.
test: Count alerts per flow; each interrupts only for essential or irreversible actions, has a specific title and verb button labels.
bad: Alert saying 'Error' with a single 'OK' for a routine tip.
good: Alert 'Delete this photo?' with Delete and Cancel.

principle: Use one prominent (primary) button for the most likely action in a view; keep prominent buttons to one or two.
test: Count visually prominent filled buttons on the screen; at most two, and the most likely action is the most prominent.
bad: Three equally filled, brightly colored buttons.
good: One filled primary, others secondary or text.

principle: Start a button label with a verb so it states what the button does, e.g. 'Add to Cart'.
test: Read each button label; it starts with a verb and names the result, with no bare 'OK', 'Submit' or 'Yes'.
bad: 'Submit', 'OK', 'Click here'.
good: 'Add to Cart', 'Send invoice'.

principle: Align elements to ease scanning and group related items with space, containers or separators.
test: Overlay edges: elements in a column share a left edge, and spacing within groups is visibly smaller than spacing between groups.
bad: Labels and fields on ragged edges; equal gaps everywhere.
good: Shared alignment edges; tight in-group, loose between-group spacing.

principle: Keep body text lines to roughly 50-75 characters (80 maximum) for readability.
test: Count characters in a full line of body text; 45-90 characters, flag > 90 or < 30.
bad: Full-width paragraph with 140 characters per line.
good: Paragraph capped around 65 characters (max-width ~ 65ch).

principle: Use a small set of type sizes (about three) so scale signals importance; more sizes dilute hierarchy.
test: List distinct font sizes on screen; more than about 4 to 5 near-duplicate sizes (e.g. 13/14/15/16) is a fail.
bad: Body text at 13, 14, 15 and 16px on one screen.
good: Small, medium, large sizes used consistently.

principle: Items close together are perceived as related; use spacing to group related items and separate unrelated ones.
test: Measure gaps: a label is closer to its own field than to the neighbor's; related controls are nearer each other than to unrelated ones.
bad: Heading equally far from the section above and below it.
good: Heading close to its content, with larger gap above.

principle: Order elements by intended importance using contrast, scale and grouping; if everything stands out, nothing does.
test: Squint/blur the screenshot; the first thing noticed is the intended primary content or action.
bad: Equal-weight bold elements; banner outshines the main task.
good: One dominant headline and one dominant action.

principle: Fitts's law: time to reach a target depends on its distance and size; make important targets large and near.
test: Check that the primary and frequent controls are large and close to where the user is acting, with space between neighbors.
bad: Tiny, tightly packed icon buttons far from the task.
good: Large primary button within thumb reach.

principle: Jakob's law: users expect your product to work like the ones they already know.
test: Compare common patterns (nav location, search icon, cart, form controls) to platform/industry conventions.
bad: Navigation hidden bottom-left; non-standard checkbox.
good: Logo top-left links home; standard controls.

principle: Hick's law (rough guide for menus): decision time grows with the number and complexity of choices; reduce or chunk options.
test: Count options presented at one decision point; > 7 to 9 ungrouped options, with no recommended one, is a flag.
bad: Menu with 20 ungrouped items.
good: Grouped menu with a highlighted recommendation.

principle: Von Restorff effect: the item that differs from similar items is most remembered; reserve distinct treatment for the key item.
source: Laws of UX: Von Restorff Effect
test: Identify visually distinct elements; each deserves its emphasis, and the key item is among them.
bad: Five badges and three accent colors all shouting.
good: Only the main CTA uses the accent color.

principle: Error messages: plain language, describe the specific problem, suggest a remedy, keep a non-blaming tone, hide codes.
test: Read each error message; it names the problem, offers a next step, has no raw code and does not blame the user.
bad: 'Something went wrong. Error 0x80070057.'
good: 'Card declined. Check the number or try another card.'

principle: Show errors near where they occur with bold, high-contrast, redundant indicators; do not rely on color alone.
test: Trigger an error; the message sits adjacent to the field and has icon or text in addition to color.
bad: Error banner at page top, field unmarked.
good: Inline message under the field with icon and text.

principle: Use plain language: short familiar words, no jargon, sentences under about 25 words, active voice.
source: GOV.UK Content and publishing guidance: Use clear language
test: Read the copy; flag long or formal words, jargon, and sentences over 25 words.
bad: 'Utilise the functionality to commence the procedure.'
good: 'Use this to start.'

principle: Make link text descriptive and front-loaded; avoid generic 'click here' or 'more'.
source: GOV.UK Content and publishing guidance: Write effective links
test: List link texts; each is meaningful out of context and unique per destination.
bad: 'Click here' for terms; 'More' x5.
good: 'Read the privacy policy'.

principle: Give the single most important action in a view one distinct, most-emphasized button style; secondary and tertiary actions get progressively less emphasis.
source: NN/g Button States: Communicate Interaction (primary, secondary, tertiary button styles)
test: Count the filled, high-emphasis buttons in each view; there is one, and it is the action the user most likely wants.
bad: Three same-colored filled buttons side by side (Submit, Cancel, Add attachment).
good: One filled primary button; Cancel is an outline or text button.

principle: Pointer targets are at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels (AAA), except inline text links, equivalents, user-agent controls and essential cases.
test: Measure the rendered size of each button, icon button and tap target on a phone-width page; each is at least 44x44 CSS px (touch target size on a mobile web page).
bad: 24px icon button with no padding next to another icon.
good: Icon button with padding so the hit area is 44x44 px.

principle: Status messages (saved, results found, error count, progress) are exposed programmatically through role or properties so assistive technology announces them without moving focus.
test: Trigger an action that shows a status message (save confirmation, toast, search result count); the message element has role=status, role=alert or aria-live so a screen reader announces it without focus moving. A status message after saving that is not announced fails.
bad: A "Saved" toast injected into a plain div; screen readers say nothing.
good: Toast has role="status" (or aria-live="polite") and is announced.

principle: When a component receives keyboard focus, no part of it is hidden by author-created content such as sticky headers, cookie banners or chat widgets (AAA).
test: Tab through the page with sticky headers, footers and banners visible; every focused control is fully visible, not partly covered.
bad: Focused link is half hidden under a sticky header.
good: Scroll-padding keeps the focused control fully in view.

principle: The keyboard focus indicator is at least a 2 CSS px perimeter of the component and has at least 3:1 contrast between focused and unfocused states (AAA).
test: Tab to each control; the focus indicator is clearly visible, at least 2px thick around the component, and contrasts 3:1 with the unfocused look.
bad: Faint 1px light-gray outline on a white page.
good: 2px solid outline in a color with 3:1 contrast and an offset.

principle: Short headlines and captions should not end with an orphaned single word; balance line lengths (for example CSS text-wrap: balance).
source: MDN: text-wrap-style (balance, for headings, captions and blockquotes)
test: Look at every multi-line headline at each viewport width; the last line holds more than one short word and line lengths are similar.
bad: Two-line headline whose second line is a single word.
good: Headline wraps into two even lines.

principle: The landing page says what the product is, what it does and why to choose it, at a glance, in specific words a competitor could not claim.
test: Show only the first screen to a newcomer for 10 seconds; they can say what it is, who it is for and what makes it different. Swap in a competitor name: the copy no longer fits.
bad: "Welcome. We empower teams to unlock their potential."
good: "Invoicing for freelance designers: send, track and get paid in one place."

principle: Use the same label for the same action or object everywhere in a flow; do not rename it between screens.
source: NN/g UI Copy: UX Guidelines for Command Names and Keyboard Shortcuts
test: List the label for each action and object across the screens of a flow (button, heading, confirmation, error); one name per thing.
bad: Button says "Create project", the page title says "New workspace", the toast says "Site added".
good: "Project" on the button, title and toast.

principle: Back trust claims with specific, verifiable evidence (named customers, third-party reviews, real numbers, contact details) instead of vague claims.
source: NN/g Trustworthiness in Web Design: 4 Credibility Factors
test: For each trust claim (logos, testimonials, ratings, security badges), check it names who, how many or where it can be verified, ideally on an external site.
bad: "Trusted by thousands of happy customers" with unnamed stock-photo quotes.
good: "4.7 on G2 from 612 reviews" linking to the G2 page; named customer with company.

principle: Start headings and link text with the words that carry the most information, since scanning readers mostly see the first two words.
source: NN/g First 2 Words: A Signal for the Scanning Eye
test: Read only the first two words of each heading and link in a list; each still signals what it is about.
bad: Links: "Click here to see pricing", "Learn about our plans".
good: Links: "Pricing plans", "Plan comparison".
